title: Diwali Without Overeating: A Mumbai Nutritionist's Three-Item Plate Rule
excerpt: Senior nutritionist Jinal Shah backs a three-item plate — protein, vegetables, and one carbohydrate or treat — so Diwali favourites stay on the menu without the overeating.
body:
• Senior nutritionist Jinal Shah, associated with Team Rujuta Diwekar, backs a "three-item plate rule" for Diwali: only three items on the plate at a time — a protein, a fibre-rich vegetable, and a carbohydrate or one festive treat.
  • The rule is a portion cue, not a ban: traditional sweets made fresh are to be enjoyed in moderation, with second helpings only when you are genuinely still hungry.
  • Do not skip meals to "save room" for a party — Mumbai clinicians and Apollo Hospitals' Navi Mumbai nutritionist Varsha Gorey both warn that arriving hungry leads to overeating.
  • Choose water, herbal tea or thin chaas over sugary, carbonated drinks, which a Mumbai gastroenterologist says amplify bloating and heartburn alongside rich food.

Diwali tables make overeating easy: samosas, kachoris, namkeens and mithai arrive in round after round of family visits. This Diwali, Mumbai health professionals are promoting a simpler discipline than calorie counting — the "three-item plate rule," spotlighted in a Free Press Journal report and detailed by Health and Family. The idea is to put only three distinct items on your plate at a time, so the favourites stay on the menu but portions police themselves.

The three tips, as the nutritionist frames them

1. Anchor the plate with protein. One of the three items should be a protein-rich food — dal, paneer, unflavoured curd, chickpeas, rajma, eggs or lean meat. Protein is the anchor that keeps a festive plate filling rather than purely indulgent.

2. Add a fibre-rich vegetable. The second item is a seasonal salad, a stir-fried sabzi or lightly cooked greens. Fibre and micronutrients slow the meal down and balance the fried and sweet items around it — a plate of tadka dal, bhindi sabzi and a phulka is the report's own example.

3. Keep the third slot for a carbohydrate — or one festive treat. The final item is a roti, a measured portion of rice or millets, or a single festive delicacy such as one samosa or one laddoo. An evening snack can follow the same pattern: a samosa paired with cucumber salad and a bowl of curd, rather than a plate piled with eight to ten items at once.

Senior nutritionist Jinal Shah, associated with Team Rujuta Diwekar, argues in the report that festive eating should not be reduced to clinical calorie counting. Traditional foods, she notes, carry cultural meaning, and swapping beloved regional sweets for commercial products marketed as "sugar-free" or "guilt-free" can introduce artificial ingredients that upset digestion more than the original mithai. Her advice is to relish authentic, freshly made sweets in moderation, hold to the three-item boundary, and take a second helping only when genuine physical hunger persists.

Why the gut protests

Dr Dattatray Solanke, consultant gastroenterologist at Kokilaben Dhirubhai Ambani Hospital in Mumbai, pointed out in the same report that excessive intake of rich, fatty foods frequently triggers prolonged bloating, upper abdominal fullness and sluggish digestion, because large fatty meals delay the rate at which food leaves the stomach. Pairing rich snacks with sugary, carbonated beverages or alcohol, he cautioned, amplifies abdominal distension and heartburn, particularly for people with existing digestive sensitivity.

Habits that make the rule work

The guidance around the rule is as practical as the rule itself:

  • Keep regular meal timings. Fasting through breakfast and lunch to "save calories" for an evening party leads to extreme hunger and overeating at night. Apollo Hospitals' festive eating guide, verified by clinical nutritionist Varsha Gorey of Apollo Hospitals, Navi Mumbai, makes the same point: do not skip meals, because skipping leads to overeating later.
  • Drink water first. Thirst is often misread as hunger. Plain water, infused herbal teas or thin chaas are the recommended drinks over sodas and sweetened punches; Gorey's guide likewise advises drinking plenty of water and keeping portions small with smaller bites.
  • Leave a gap before bed and walk a little. A buffer of two to three hours between dinner and sleep reduces night-time reflux, and a gentle 15-minute walk after a meal aids digestion — advice Gorey's guide echoes with its recommendation of a short walk or light stretching.

The experts are careful about the limits: the three-item rule is a behavioural cue, not a medical prescription, and no clinical trials show that eating exactly three items by itself prevents weight gain. Its value is that it forces a deliberate choice before each serving. The framing fits the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024), which favour dietary diversification — energy spread across legumes, whole grains, vegetables and nuts. For diaspora households celebrating this weekend: plate three things, enjoy the mithai you actually love, and let the next plate be a decision rather than a reflex. People with conditions requiring medical nutrition therapy should follow their clinician's guidance over any general festive rule.
